How Long Does It Take to Charge an EV? Quick Answer

To find EV charging time, work out how many kilowatt-hours you need to add, then divide by the effective charging power. A 60 kWh battery charging from 20% to 80% needs to absorb 36 kWh (60 × 0.60). On a 7.4 kW Level 2 charger at 90% efficiency the pack effectively receives about 6.66 kW, so the charge takes roughly 5.4 hours. The calculator above returns this instantly along with the energy added and the time in minutes.

The most common mistake is dividing the whole battery size by the charger rating and stopping there. Real charge time depends on the state-of-charge window you actually drive through — most people top up from 20–30% to 80%, not from empty to full — and on charging losses that mean not every watt from the wall reaches the cells. Building both into the number gives you a plan you can trust for an overnight charge or a road-trip stop.

f(x)

The EV Charging Time Formula Explained

The equation used by this calculator is:

Charging Time (hours) = (Battery kWh × (End SOC − Start SOC) ÷ 100) ÷ (Charger kW × Efficiency)

Each term controls the result:

  • Battery kWh — usable pack capacity. A car marketed as "64 kWh" often has a usable figure a little lower; use the usable number when you know it.
  • State of charge (SOC) — the percentage window you are filling. Charging 20→80% moves 60% of the pack; 10→100% moves 90%. Battery preconditioning and the automaker's charge limit both live here.
  • Charger kW — the real delivered power, which is the lower of the charger's output and the car's onboard AC charger. A 7.4 kW wallbox feeding a car with a 7.2 kW onboard charger delivers 7.2 kW.
  • Efficiency (η) — AC-to-DC conversion in the onboard charger, plus battery thermal management. Level 2 AC charging is roughly 85–92% efficient; DC fast charging bypasses the onboard charger and is efficient at the pack but tapers hard near the top.

Because a kilowatt-hour of energy divided by a kilowatt of power yields hours, the units resolve cleanly to time. To turn that time into a dollar figure, pair this with the EV charging cost calculator, and to size the circuit and breaker your charger needs, use the home EV charger amp calculator.

Worked Examples: Real EV Charging Scenarios

These examples show how the SOC window and charger choice reshape the same battery's charge time.

Example 1 — 60 kWh crossover, 20→80% on a home Level 2 charger: Energy added = 60 × 0.60 = 36 kWh. Effective power at 7.4 kW and 90% efficiency = 6.66 kW. Time = 36 ÷ 6.66 = 5.4 hours — a comfortable overnight charge that leaves a healthy 80% buffer for battery longevity.

Example 2 — 75 kWh sedan, 10→100% on an 11 kW charger: Energy added = 75 × 0.90 = 67.5 kWh. Effective power = 11 × 0.90 = 9.9 kW. Time = 67.5 ÷ 9.9 = 6.8 hours. Filling the last 20% takes disproportionately long in the real world because AC charging holds steady but many owners reserve 100% only for trips.

Example 3 — 82 kWh SUV, 30→80% on Level 1 (120 V) overnight: Energy added = 82 × 0.50 = 41 kWh. Effective power at 1.4 kW and 85% efficiency = 1.19 kW. Time = 41 ÷ 1.19 = 34.5 hours. This is why Level 1 is a trickle: fine for a plug-in hybrid or a low-mileage commuter, impractical for a big battery.

Example 4 — DC fast charge, 60 kWh, 20→80% at an average 60 kW: Energy added = 36 kWh. At 60 kW average delivered power (fast chargers taper, so the peak is higher), time ≈ 36 ÷ 60 = 0.6 hours, about 36 minutes. DC charging skips the onboard AC charger, so we treat efficiency as near the pack; the taper above 80% is why fast-charge sessions usually stop at 80%.

↕

Why 20% to 80% Is the Charging Sweet Spot

Almost every EV maker and battery engineer recommends daily charging in a 20–80% window, and it changes the time math in a useful way. Lithium-ion cells age fastest when held at very high or very low state of charge, so avoiding the top and bottom of the pack extends calendar and cycle life. It also happens to be the fastest, most efficient region of the charge curve on DC.

On DC fast charging the difference is dramatic. Charging 20→80% might take 30–40 minutes, but pushing on from 80→100% can take almost as long again because the current tapers sharply to protect the cells. That is why road-trip planning is built around 10–80% legs, not full charges. On AC Level 2 the taper is far gentler, so filling to 100% occasionally for a long trip is fine.

The practical takeaway: set your car's charge limit to 80% for daily use and only schedule 100% right before departure. Use this calculator with your typical window — most owners find a nightly 30→80% top-up on a Level 2 charger takes only 2–4 hours, easily covered by an overnight or off-peak schedule. To see what that costs on a time-of-use plan, run the EV charging cost calculator.

How to Use the EV Charging Time Calculator

  1. Enter battery capacity in kWh. Use the usable capacity from your spec sheet if available; the marketed "gross" figure will slightly overstate charge time.
  2. Enter charger power in kW. Use the lower of your wallbox output and the car's onboard AC charger. Common values are 1.4 kW (Level 1), 7.4–11.5 kW (home Level 2), or the average delivered kW for a DC session.
  3. Set the start and end state of charge. These are the percentages shown on the dashboard. A 20→80% window is the practical default for daily charging.
  4. Set charging efficiency. Use 90% for typical Level 2 AC charging, 85% for cold-weather or heavily loaded conditions, or 95%+ for DC fast charging measured at the pack.

The result updates live in hours and minutes. Adjust the charger power to compare a 7.4 kW versus 11.5 kW wallbox, or change the SOC window to see how much time the final 20% really costs. If you are still choosing hardware, the home EV charger amp calculator shows the amps and breaker each option requires, and the EV range calculator estimates the miles each charge delivers.

What Slows Real EV Charging Down

The formula gives a clean number, but several real-world factors push actual charge time longer, especially on fast chargers.

Onboard charger limit. A car's AC charging speed is capped by its onboard charger, not the wallbox. Plug a 7.2 kW car into an 11.5 kW charger and it still charges at 7.2 kW. Always use the lower of the two figures.

Temperature and preconditioning. Cold packs charge slowly because the battery management system limits current to protect the cells. Many EVs precondition the battery when navigating to a fast charger, warming it for peak speed. In freezing weather without preconditioning, DC charge times can double.

The charge curve and taper. DC fast charging is fastest at low state of charge and tapers as the pack fills. A car that peaks at 150 kW at 20% may be down to 50 kW by 80%. That is why we use an average delivered kW for DC estimates rather than the headline peak.

Shared and derated stations. Two cars sharing a fast-charge cabinet can each get half power. Hot ambient temperatures also make some stations derate to protect their own electronics. For home AC charging none of this applies — the steady, predictable power is exactly why overnight charging is the backbone of EV ownership.

Home Overnight vs Public Fast Charging Strategy

The smartest charging strategy uses the two systems for what each does best, and the time math makes the case.

Home Level 2 for daily driving. Most drivers cover 30–40 miles a day, which a 7.4–11.5 kW home charger replaces in one to two hours overnight — well within an off-peak window. Because the car sits parked anyway, slow steady charging is free time and is gentle on the battery. Size the circuit with the home EV charger amp calculator, then estimate the running cost with the electricity cost calculator.

DC fast charging for trips. On the road, minutes matter and battery aging over a few sessions does not. Planning 10–80% legs keeps each stop near the fast part of the charge curve, typically 20–40 minutes. Beyond 80%, the taper makes it faster to drive on and stop again than to wait for a full charge.

Level 1 as a backstop. A standard 120 V outlet adds only 3–5 miles per hour, but for a plug-in hybrid or a very low-mileage EV it can be enough, and it needs no installation. Enter 1.4 kW above to see whether a trickle charge keeps up with your daily miles.

!

Common Mistakes in Charging Time Estimates

  • Using the charger rating instead of the car's onboard limit. AC speed is capped by the slower of the two — a common reason a new wallbox feels no faster.
  • Charging from empty to full in your estimate. Daily charging almost never uses the whole pack; a 20→80% window is both realistic and faster.
  • Ignoring efficiency losses. 8–15% of the energy from the wall never reaches the cells on AC; leaving it out understates both time and cost.
  • Expecting peak DC speed the whole session. Fast charging tapers; use an average delivered kW, not the headline number.
  • Forgetting cold-weather derating. A cold pack charges slowly until preconditioned — plan extra time in winter.

For a full picture of a charge session, combine this tool with the EV charging cost calculator and the battery charge time calculator for 12 V and auxiliary batteries.

Methodology, Review Notes, and Sources

How this calculator works

The calculator finds the energy that must move into the pack — battery capacity times the change in state of charge — then divides by the effective charging power, which is the charger rating multiplied by charging efficiency. Charging efficiency accounts for AC-to-DC conversion, thermal management, and onboard-charger losses, typically 85–92% for Level 2 AC charging.

FAQ

EV Charging Time Calculator — FAQ

Fast answers before you rely on the calculator.

Q1 How long does it take to charge an electric car?

It depends on battery size, charger power, and the state-of-charge window. A 60 kWh EV charging 20→80% on a 7.4 kW Level 2 charger takes about 5.4 hours; on an 11.5 kW charger about 3.5 hours; on a DC fast charger averaging 60 kW about 36 minutes. Level 1 (120 V) can take a full day or more for a large pack.

Q2 How long to charge an EV from 20% to 80%?

Charging 20→80% moves 60% of the battery. For a 60 kWh pack that is 36 kWh. At 7.4 kW and 90% efficiency it takes about 5.4 hours; at 11.5 kW about 3.5 hours; at a 60 kW DC average about 36 minutes. The 20–80% window is recommended because it charges fastest on DC and is gentlest on battery life.

Q3 Why is my EV charging slower than the calculator says?

The most common cause is the car's onboard AC charger being slower than the wallbox — AC speed is capped by the lower of the two. Cold temperatures, a battery that has not preconditioned, a shared or derated public station, and the DC taper above 80% also slow real charging. Lower the efficiency input or use the average delivered kW for a more realistic estimate.

Q4 Does charging to 100% take longer per percent?

On DC fast charging, yes — the current tapers sharply above 80% to protect the cells, so the last 20% can take almost as long as the first 60%. On AC Level 2 charging the power stays roughly constant, so each percent takes about the same time. This is why road trips are planned around 10–80% legs.

Q5 What charging efficiency should I use?

Use about 90% for typical Level 2 AC charging, 85% for cold weather or heavily loaded conditions, and 95% or higher for DC fast charging measured at the pack. The losses come from AC-to-DC conversion in the onboard charger and battery thermal management, so DC charging (which bypasses the onboard charger) is more efficient at the battery.

Q6 How much faster is an 11.5 kW charger than a 7.4 kW charger?

Roughly 55% faster on AC, if the car can accept the full power. A 60 kWh 20→80% charge takes about 5.4 hours at 7.4 kW versus about 3.5 hours at 11.5 kW. The gain only materializes if the car's onboard charger supports 11.5 kW; many EVs cap at 7.2–7.7 kW, in which case the faster wallbox makes no difference.

Q7 Can I charge an EV overnight on a normal outlet?

You can, but a standard 120 V Level 1 outlet only delivers about 1.4 kW, adding 3–5 miles of range per hour. Over an 8-hour night that is roughly 25–40 miles — enough for a short commuter or a plug-in hybrid, but not enough to refill a large battery. Most EV owners install a 240 V Level 2 charger for practical daily charging.
